source: Belloni, Chen, Wei (2026) Online Pandora's Box for Contextual LLM Cascading
finding: Gap 1. Learns Weitzman reservation indices online for choosing which LLM API to query next and when to stop. In simulation the Weitzman-based policies beat FrugalGPT (a fixed cascade) and one-shot contextual bandits.
numbers: Simulation only: 3 APIs, 30,000 periods, 100-dim contexts, 3 environments x 2 regimes. Oracle queries 1.30-1.78 boxes per period. Gap between known- and unknown-reward variants at most about 0.17% of oracle utility. FrugalGPT comparable only in one regime with a large warm start (n0=1000); substantially worse at small warm start and in Regime B.
limits: Simulated rewards, no real LLM outputs. Authors say formal guarantees do not directly apply to the indices tested.
agent_relevance: Index ordering beats a fixed order when the best order depends on context. Supports the K01 agent test, but on API choice, not tool calls or hypothesis checks.

source: Cinquin, Pleiss, Kristiadi (2025) Limits of PRM-Guided Tree Search for Mathematical Reasoning with LLMs
finding: Gap 1 and 6. A Gittins-index sampling rule (keep sampling a state only while expected improvement over the current best exceeds cost) was tried inside PRM-guided tree search. It gave no gain over best-of-N.
numbers: 23 math problems, Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct. Mean accuracy: Greedy@6 71.6, Greedy@20 71.2, Beam@4 71.8-71.9, MCTS@8 71.2, Gittins@0.05 70.5, Gittins@linear 71.4, GBFS@8 46.0. PRM-guided tree search shows no significant gain over BoN at higher cost.
limits: One small model, one PRM. Authors blame the PRM: it poorly approximates state value and gets worse with depth, so an index built on it inherits the error.
agent_relevance: An index rule is only as good as its value estimate. A marginal-value abandon rule on branches needs a calibrated value signal first.

source: Harris and Slivkins (2026, v3) Should You Use Your Large Language Model to Explore or Exploit?
finding: Gap 4. Tests LLMs separately as exploitation and exploration oracles in contextual bandits. Reasoning models (GPT-5 family) exploit best but are slow and expensive. Tool use and summaries help on medium tasks. All LLMs still lose to simple linear regression, even on non-linear tasks.
numbers: Models: GPT-5.2, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Qwen-2.5, Gemma-3, Mistral-7B, DeepSeek-R1. As explorers proposing candidate arms: LLM rewards 0.5-0.6 on a contrarian-answers task versus random below 0.1; best for K=3 or 4 candidates.
limits: Separates explore from exploit, so it does not re-test the combined in-context failure of Krishnamurthy. Two reasoning models dropped for short context.
agent_relevance: Reasoning helps but does not remove the failure. LLM as proposer plus an external algorithm for the exploit and stop step is the robust split.

source: Arumugam and Griffiths (ICLR 2026) Toward Efficient Exploration by Large Language Model Agents
finding: Gap 4. Implements posterior sampling (PSRL) with LLM sub-calls instead of asking the LLM to explore implicitly. In a stochastic-transition task, swapping GPT-4o for o1-mini turned linear regret into regret on par with classic PSRL.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1 improves all LLM agents but not significantly over LLM-based PSRL (reported in the text).
limits: Model upgrade mattered in one stochastic environment. Authors argue for an external algorithm rather than in-context imitation.
agent_relevance: The fix came from an explicit external algorithm plus a stronger model, not from the model exploring on its own.

source: Wang, Yan et al. (2026) Think Longer to Explore Deeper: Length-Incentivized RL
finding: Gap 4 and 6. Names a Shallow Exploration Trap: long traces that cover many states are exponentially unlikely under autoregressive sampling. A length reward plus redundancy penalty (LIE) in RL raises in-context exploration.
numbers: Average in-domain gain 4.4% and out-of-domain 2.7% (Qwen3, Llama); versus GSPO: 1.7B +7.6%, 4B +4.4%, 8B +2.5%; 8B OOD 73.4% (+2.9).
limits: Training-based, outside our no-training scope. Gains are small. Measures reasoning benchmarks, not bandit regret.
agent_relevance: Suggests reasoning models do not explore broadly by default; a scaffold must force alternatives rather than hope.

source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Gap 2 and 6. Uses the model's own token confidence to stop or drop low-confidence reasoning traces early, with no reward model and no training. Online mode is an abandon-the-branch rule.
numbers: AIME 2025, GPT-OSS-120B offline: 99.9% vs 97.0% majority@512 vs 91.8% pass@1. Online: tokens cut up to 84.7%. DeepConf-low cuts 43-79% tokens (DeepSeek-8B AIME24 +5.8% accuracy; Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 -0.9%). DeepConf-high cuts 18-59% with near-identical accuracy.
limits: Authors report overconfidence on wrong problems (GPT-OSS-120B), where aggressive top-10% filtering can hurt; the 90% setting is safer. Math tasks with a single answer only. Baseline is full majority voting, not fixed-depth truncation at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Confidence-only stopping works on math but fails where the model is confidently wrong.

source: Taubenfeld, Sheffer et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: Gap 2. Weights votes by the model's own confidence score. Needs no external reward model. Beats plain self-consistency in nearly all configurations.
numbers: Nine models, four datasets; over 40% fewer reasoning paths on average; example Gemma2-9B on MATH: 73% cost reduction at equal accuracy.
limits: Weighted voting, not a stopping rule. Gains rest on within-question confidence ranking; the authors stress that absolute confidence across questions is poorly calibrated.
agent_relevance: Within-question confidence ranking is usable as an acceptance signal; absolute confidence across questions is not.

finding: Gap 2. Stops sampling when a Bayesian stopping criterion says the current majority is very likely stable. No reward model; acceptance comes from agreement among samples.
numbers: Reduces sample budget by up to 7.9 times with average accuracy drop under 0.1%.
limits: Needs repeated answers that can be compared; not for open-ended text. Assumes samples are independent.
agent_relevance: Agreement among samples is the cheapest no-reward-model acceptance signal. Same family as ESC (K07).

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: Gap 6. Training-free: at reasoning transition points the model is prompted for a trial answer, and thinking stops if confidence in it is high. A marginal-value stop rule for a single chain.
numbers: 10 benchmarks, 11 reasoning models: chain-of-thought length cut by 19.1% to 80.1% on average with accuracy change +0.3% to +5.0%. About 75% of samples contain an early correct answer.
limits: Compared with unrestricted reasoning, not with a fixed token cap at equal budget.
agent_relevance: Early exit on a single chain saves tokens and sometimes raises accuracy; supports checking at transitions and stopping when the trial answer is stable.

source: Damani, Shenfeld et al. (2024) Learning How Hard to Think: Input-Adaptive Allocation of LM Computation
finding: Gap 5. A lightweight probe on the model's hidden states predicts how much extra samples will help, with no oracle label at test time. Allocating budget by this prediction cuts compute or lifts quality.
numbers: Up to 50% less compute at the same quality (code), or up to 10% higher quality at fixed budget; chat best-of-k matches reward with up to 10% less compute.
limits: Probe is trained with reward labels offline. Needs hidden-state access, not available for closed APIs. Gains smallest on chat.
agent_relevance: Per-prompt difficulty is predictable from the model's own state; for API-only agents the substitute is pilot samples (agreement rate), which costs tokens.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally (model-predicted difficulty)
finding: Gap 5. Snell tested oracle difficulty bins (ground truth) and model-predicted bins (from PRM scores, same 2048 samples per problem). With predicted bins the gains shrink at higher budgets but remain at low budgets.
numbers: With PRM search, compute-optimal allocation matches best-of-N with up to 4x less test-time compute (16 vs 64 generations) at low budgets; benefits diminish with predicted difficulty at higher budgets.
limits: Authors say the difficulty estimate itself costs inference and leave the balance to future work; the experiments do not charge for it.
agent_relevance: The oracle-free version is weaker and its cost was not charged in the headline numbers.

source: Chawla, Gergatsouli, Teng, Tzamos, Zhang (2020) Pandora's Box with Correlations: Learning and Approximation
finding: Gap 7. Weitzman's rule assumes independent boxes. With correlated values, fully adaptive strategies cannot be efficiently approximated within any sub-linear factor from samples. Simple partially adaptive strategies (fixed probe order, adaptive stop) are constant-factor approximate to the best partially adaptive one.
numbers: Theory: tight within constant factors; polynomial sample complexity. No empirical cost-of-independence number.
limits: Worst-case theory; says nothing about typical LLM hypothesis sets.
agent_relevance: No known cheap fix for correlated hypotheses. Practical reading: fixed probe order plus adaptive stopping is the provable fallback.

source: Xie, Astudillo, Frazier, Scully, Terenin (2024-2026) Cost-aware Bayesian Optimization via the Pandora's Box Gittins Index
finding: Gap 1 and 7. Turns Weitzman's index into an acquisition rule with a stopping rule for Bayesian optimisation, optimal for the cost-per-sample independent case and used as a heuristic otherwise. Authors report it performs well, particularly in medium-high dimensions.
numbers: Only the abstract-level claim was read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not an LLM study. Optimality needs the independent structure.
agent_relevance: Shows an index heuristic can work when values are correlated through a model; no LLM test.

source: Kalayci et al. (2025) Optimal Stopping vs Best-of-N for Inference Time Optimization
finding: Gap 2 and 8. Stopping thresholds are learned online from rewards with anytime-valid confidence bounds, with rewards normalised across prompts. Acceptance depends on a reward model r.
numbers: 15-35% fewer generations than best-of-N, 1,600 profiles, win rate above 54% (cross-checked earlier).
limits: Utility is defined by a reward model; no self-confidence variant tested. Thresholds adapt within a run, not transferred across tasks.
agent_relevance: Closest to learning thresholds on the fly. No test of reusing thresholds across tasks; no-reward-model analogues are d06-d08.

source: Horton (2023) Large Language Models as Simulated Economic Agents: What Can We Learn from Homo Silicus?
finding: Gap 9. Simulated LLM subjects replicate several classic economics results (for example a minimum-wage hiring shift). The paper has no McCall or Stigler search experiment and measures no regret against a search optimum.
limits: Text search of the paper found no sequential-search experiment. Results described as suggestive.
agent_relevance: Keeps K11 gap open: no LLM measurement of stopping against the reservation optimum was found.

source: Nie et al. (2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration (BanditBench)
finding: Gap 4. Only the abstract and intro were skimmed. Supplying UCB-style guidance at inference, or distilling UCB trajectories by demonstration or fine-tuning, lets smaller models approach the classical algorithm.
agent_relevance: External algorithm hints beat raw in-context exploration.
